source.version_note: Registered Report, Scientific Reports 16:11868; Crossref online date 19 March 2026. Supplied PDF has later May/June production metadata, which does not by itself establish a separate publication or correction.
source.verification_method: All eleven supplied pages read, including protocol deviations, 38 references and declarations. All four figures and Tables 1–3 inspected, with figures/tables on pages 4–8 also viewed as rendered images. Crossref verifies identity and online publication date. External supplements, registration, raw data and code not independently read or rerun.

citation.title: Advice quality and source disclosure shape trust in AI-generated ethical advice

reading.source_scope_note: Two human evaluations of GPT-4 versus one newspaper ethicist’s advice: a blinded pilot and a preregistered three-condition experiment with disclosed deviations. Outcomes are immediate stated source preferences and perceived usefulness, not actual advice following, independently adjudicated moral correctness or longitudinal trust.
access_limits: Entire supplied article and its printed figures/tables read. Referenced online supplementary tables/figures, prompts, data, code and the OSF Stage 1 protocol were not independently inspected.
Crossref metadata verifies article identity/date only. Referenced NYT columns and primary papers do not become fully read sources through this review.

study.pilot: September–October 2023: panel described as 18 invited ethical experts (4 pastors, 1 rabbi, 13 academics), 69 Wharton MBA students and 100 Prolific participants. Only 17 experts responded, yielding 186 reported respondents rather than the abstract’s 187. Six expert respondents rated absolute usefulness and eleven made relative choices. Repeated responses retained after <20-second removal: 110 expert, 517 Prolific, 263 MBA, total 890. Response counts are not participant counts.
study.stimuli: Twenty NYT Ethicist dilemmas and Kwame Anthony Appiah’s replies; GPT-4 prompted with one example reply to align style. A content/usefulness comparison does not isolate reasoning from rhetoric. Publication after GPT-4’s initial release is a contamination precaution, not independently verified proof of no training exposure without snapshot/cutoff details.
study.pilot_results: Absolute usefulness fixed source effect B=.11, 95% CI [-.26,.48], d=.08 [-.16,.30], p=.56: no detected difference, not formal equivalence. Relative choices overall 57% AI, OR1.34 [1.01,1.79], p<.035; laypeople 59.6%, experts 55.5% and MBA 51.3%, with the latter two nonsignificant and wide intervals. Repeated participant/dilemma random intercepts were modeled.
study.main_sample: Stage 1 accepted in principle 13 September 2024. Target 618, collected 658 before exclusions due delayed closure, retained 642: A219, B211, C212. Five dilemmas each, 3210 choices overall; pairwise models use 2150/2115 choices from 430/423 people. Ratings in B+C:4230 ratings from 423 people. These are not thousands of independent participants.
study.conditions: A saw dilemmas only and chose a preferred human-expert versus ChatGPT adviser. B saw both actual replies with truthful source labels and selected the more useful text. C saw the same replies and wording with labels withheld. A→B bundles advice exposure with changed question/estimand; B→C isolates disclosure for the supplied pair, not pure AI-label assignment to an otherwise identical single text.
study.main_results: AI-favoring response shares A27.4%, B46.8%, C53.7%; A→B difference 19.4 percentage points, mixed-model OR2.62 [2.05,3.35], p<.001; B→C difference 6.9 points, OR1.38 [1.10,1.73], p=.005. These are between-group differences, not within-person improvement or universal rates of ethical behavior.
study.exploratory_ratings: Source × disclosure B≈−.395, d≈−.25, p<.001. Human-minus-AI usefulness when disclosed≈+.284; blinded≈−.111, p=.082. Main coefficient pattern supports human=1 coding, contrary to caption. Four of 20 dilemmas reverse the A→B pattern; lower emotional load and greater human directiveness are post hoc explanations, not manipulated causes.
study.protocol_deviations: Paper explicitly reports oversampling, replacing intended prefer-to-follow wording in B/C with more-useful-text wording, and omitted post-dilemma attention checks due programming errors. Only initial comprehension check administered. Planned timing exclusion appears in Table 1; implementation details cannot be independently reconstructed without data/code.
study.interpretive_boundary: Natural-language arguments, anthropomorphic familiarity, transparency and perceived competence are proposed mechanisms, not tested mediators. Ratings do not demonstrate faithful model reasoning, consciousness, ethical authority, valid consent or improved clinical/legal outcomes.

summary: No new catalogue row: enrich algorithm aversion with a randomized source-disclosure comparison and preserve boundaries around algorithm appreciation, epistemic/moral trust, calibration and anthropomorphism. Record the disclosed survey deviations and verified internal reporting errors instead of treating attractiveness or uptake as ethical correctness.

findings.definition: Reluctance to use or accept algorithmic judgments relative to human judgment in a comparable task.
findings.novelty_rationale: The paper explicitly tests this existing construct; the disclosure contrast adds evidence without adding a new name for source-related evaluation.
findings.evidence_scope: Randomized B/C arms show AI-favoring reply choices 46.8% with source labels versus 53.7% blinded, OR1.38[1.10,1.73]. A27.4% versus B46.8% also differs, but changed adviser-preference versus text-usefulness wording confounds a quality-only interpretation. Five repeated choices/person are modeled with participant/dilemma intercepts.
findings.boundary: These are immediate preference/usefulness responses, not actual following or moral correctness. A human-source preference may be justified. Disclosure labels both AI and the expert; it does not randomize a label onto identical text. Preserve item-level reversals and the authors’ disclosed programming deviations.

findings.definition: Giving greater weight or preference to algorithmic than human advice in a comparable task.
findings.novelty_rationale: Keep content preference without source knowledge separate from a positive effect of knowing the source is algorithmic.
findings.evidence_scope: The blinded pilot’s 57% preference and blinded main condition’s 53.7% preference favor AI-authored texts, but cannot identify algorithm-source appreciation because respondents do not know the provenance. Treat as a boundary comparison, not a demonstrated source-appreciation effect.
findings.boundary: Human and AI replies differ in content and residual rhetoric. Blinded preference is not liking algorithms, objective superiority, overconfidence or transfer of moral accountability.

findings.definition: Relying on an adviser as a source of knowledge because of perceived competence or reasoning ability.
findings.novelty_rationale: The title’s trust terminology should not silently convert text usefulness into observed knowledge reliance.
findings.evidence_scope: No epistemic-trust scale, actual reliance task or mediated competence mechanism is reported. Usefulness and adviser choice are relevant neighboring outcomes, but do not directly establish this broader construct.
findings.boundary: A credible-sounding argument can be mistaken; perceived expertise, truth, transparency and actual reliance remain separate. Do not count a boundary-only note as a new measured trust paper.

findings.definition: Willingness to endorse the values or ethical commitments attributed to an adviser.
findings.novelty_rationale: The study evaluates advice usefulness rather than directly assessing endorsement of an adviser’s values.

evidence.quote: which of the two pieces of advice is more useful

findings.evidence_scope: The moral topic and trust language do not supply a moral-trust measure in the ontology’s values-endorsement sense. No new estimate of moral trust is extracted.
findings.boundary: A useful answer, source preference or moral agreement on one dilemma does not establish broader values endorsement or actual moral character.

findings.definition: Using assistance to a degree justified by its task-specific competence, relevance, uncertainty and error consequences.
findings.novelty_rationale: The study increases measured preference without testing whether reliance tracks independently warranted advice quality.
findings.evidence_scope: No good/bad advice manipulation with a defensible correctness benchmark, behavior-under-error task or longitudinal reliance calibration is tested. The source-disclosure effect cannot establish appropriate trust.
findings.boundary: Uptake is not calibration. A disclosure intervention that increases acceptance could improve or worsen decisions depending on actual content and context.

findings.definition: Attributing human characteristics or mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Human-like linguistic familiarity is an author-proposed mechanism, not a measured explanation for the observed source effect.

evidence.quote: do not attest to the mechanisms

findings.evidence_scope: The discussion proposes more-human appearance and transparent-seeming thought as pathways but measures neither anthropomorphic attribution nor causal mediation.
findings.boundary: Natural-language readability and human-like style are not proof that respondents attributed mental states or that a model has conscious moral experience.

source_corrections.issue: Caption calls A absolute and B relative, but rendered panel A shows choice probability and panel B mean usefulness.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: A depicts the relative choice condition; B depicts absolute usefulness ratings.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Rendered figure, axis labels and methods/results checked directly.

source_corrections.issue: Caption codes source 1=AI/0=human and says positive coefficients favor AI, while the table labels Expert=1 and the prose reports positive human-minus-AI difference.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Interpret the displayed .284 as human-expert minus AI usefulness in the disclosed condition; the −.395 interaction changes this difference to approximately −.111 when blinded. Caption source coding/direction must match the table and prose.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Internal table/prose arithmetic, not raw-data or code reproduction.

source_corrections.location: PDF page 3, absolute pilot confidence-interval interpretation
source_corrections.issue: Text says interval excludes effects of |d|<.16 in favor of the human rater, despite reporting d interval[-.16,.30].
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The reported interval includes zero and effects smaller than .16 in magnitude; it bounds a human advantage at about .16 on the paper’s AI-minus-human sign convention. It does not establish equivalence.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Interpretation of the printed interval only; rater/advice terminology also differs.

source_corrections.location: PDF page 5, MBA relative-choice odds-ratio interval
source_corrections.issue: B=.06, coefficient CI[-.29,.41], but OR CI printed [.95,1.51].
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Exponentiating the printed coefficient interval gives approximately [.75,1.51], not [.95,1.51]. Which original value is wrong cannot be resolved without model output.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Arithmetic consistency check, not a replacement estimate from raw data.

source_corrections.location: PDF page 1 abstract versus page 3 expert response count
source_corrections.issue: Abstract pilot N187 includes all 18 invited experts, although methods report only 17 responded alongside 69 MBA and 100 Prolific.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The described respondent total is 186. Retain uncertainty about reported N rather than invent an eighteenth response.

source_corrections.issue: Stimulus-plots sentence cites references 36–37, which are SIMR power analysis and lme 4; the named stimulus-sampling paper is reference 38.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Reference 38 is the listed methodological source for stimulus plots.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Printed bibliography and in-text citation only; cited methods papers not independently read.

methodological_limits: One human columnist and one GPT-4 prompting setup across twenty selected dilemmas; trained ethics judgment, cultural coverage and performance in high-stakes decisions are not established by this stimulus sample.

A→B is a randomized bundled contrast with a changed outcome question, explicitly acknowledged by the authors. It cannot identify advice quality/exposure alone. B→C tests disclosure on evaluations of the same two underlying replies.
No detected usefulness difference, small expert/MBA subgroups and rounded response shares do not constitute formal equivalence, universal expert superiority or reliable individual moral choice.
A preference for a human adviser can reflect legitimate accountability, relationship or consent concerns. Calling the difference algorithm aversion does not prove irrationality.

Higher uptake after withholding origin does not justify deceptive deployment. The paper acknowledges disclosure/manipulation concerns; no institutional authorization or ethical intervention was validated.

All claims about rhetoric, emotional loading, anthropomorphism and transparent thought processes remain hypotheses or post hoc interpretations; natural-language explanation is not proof of faithful internal process.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The normative requirement for accountable clinical judgment and this advice-usefulness experiment answer different questions. A highly rated reply does not settle moral agency or responsibility; a philosophical position does not negate the measured ratings.

Normative explanations can affect trust judgments there, while source disclosure affects usefulness/preference here. Neither immediate rating proves calibrated reliance, actual recovery in real-world behavior or objectively correct moral advice.

Accounting-study credibility was post-advice, nonrandomized as a mediator; here B→C directly randomizes source disclosure. Both still require distinctions among credibility, advice evaluation and actual conduct.

deferred.reason: Useful description of the experimental contrast but no separately established psychological mechanism is identified. Capture the source-dependent algorithm-aversion result in the existing entry rather than add another overlapping row.
Broad advice-use process and evaluation paradigm respectively; this experiment measures stated preferences/usefulness rather than actual utilization, and does not newly test source identification.
Proposed explanatory pathways, not isolated or measured constructs here; fluent prose and reasoning quality are not separated.

limitations: One article, two studies and repeated judgments do not become multiple independent source papers. No new bibliometric total, timeline series or ethical violation edge is inferred.
